--- integrated runtime ---
# Integrated harve/y runtime and lab

Implementation on `codex/harvey-integrated-runtime`, based on main `dc3a109` and lab `08274aa`.
The original development checkout and its local credentials remain separate.

## Implemented

- Unconfirmed closes raise an incomplete-session error without writing a finished journal result.
  Resume keeps the existing session. Exhausted uncertain sends retain their persisted move ID.
  Cached replies keep server-derived remaining time; worker failures reach the caller.
- Main's package policies and shared closing evaluator are retained. `economics.evaluate` rejects
  invalid prices/options/fixed-term changes/must-haves and returns full components plus demand coverage.
  Price-budget search handles non-monotonic relationship costs with bounded sampling and validates
  rounded prices. Sampling is conservative; it does not claim a global optimum.
- Versioned public ingestion records file hashes, case context and explicit source conflicts.
  Conflicting release IDs are excluded from claims. Missing optional tables produce diagnostics;
  explicit missing data paths do not silently load a different package. Contact notes and
  previously unknown suppliers are retained. Prep output includes the data manifest.
- Bounded extractive reply interpretation identifies supplier statements about hedging, payment,
  quality, clauses and authority. Verified alternative arguments replace vetoed index arguments.
  Final offers receive no new evidence decoration. This implementation uses deterministic rules,
  not an LLM or personality inference; it makes zero provider calls.
- The lab accepts embedded validated policy configurations in immutable checkpoints, so its worker
  can execute the same package policy as the normal CLI. Workers retain decision traces.
- `FeedbackAgent` audits original outcomes and conversations and emits referenced keep/change/test
  findings. Recovered scores remain separate, unknown timeouts stay unknown, and uncovered demand
  triggers a contract comparison recommendation. Matching versioned public data enables qualified
  offer checks; unknown historical versions are skipped rather than checked against today's data.
  Cross-run observations are retained as observations, never auto-approved runtime policy.
- Feedback is available from the authenticated `/api/feedback/<run_id>` read endpoint and in each
  dashboard experiment's Decision feedback disclosure. CLI audits are stored separately from
  immutable attempt records and can be regenerated.

## Use the integrated candidate

```sh
uv run --locked negotiator play case:D01 --runner async --policy-config configs/candidate.json
uv run --locked negotiator lab feedback --data "$ARENA_DATA"
```

The first command starts a free hosted sandbox session when configured for the arena. The second
only audits the local lab database. Do not run practice as an incidental verification command.

For a lab checkpoint, pass `configs/harvey-lab-checkpoint.json` as the config and select `--runner async`.
Use the explicit `configs/lab-async-sandbox-suite.json` suite and a matching base data manifest.
That suite has three repeats per case per arm: twelve free sandbox sessions, not two. Publication,
baseline seeding, family budget and campaign execution remain explicit actions using the lab CLI.
The committed base hash matches the audited kit data; a new release requires a new manifest/suite.

Local end-to-end rehearsal:

```sh
uv run --locked python tools/rehearse_loop.py --runner async \
  --policy configs/candidate.json --data "$ARENA_DATA"
```

This creates an isolated temporary lab, local Git remote and kit simulator, then runs twelve local
sessions through restored checkpoints. It does not change the shared lab recommendation or use
hosted quota. Its deliberately weak control tests integration, not production competitiveness.

## Imported evidence

The integration checkout's ignored `experiments/dashboard.sqlite3` contains 100 run records / 113
attempts: the two saved practice sweeps (15 attempts), plus 53 sandbox and 45 additional practice
sessions read from owned history. Fifteen existing practice sessions were deduplicated. No import
failures. Original source/config is unknown for server-only history, and the importer is not the
original author. P10's operator-assisted recovery preserves its original failed execution.

This is a local database. It has not replaced Barış's running shared database or deployed the UI.
Use the existing lab sync workflow with the team's configured destination when publishing records.
Keep credentials and the local derived feedback JSON out of Git.

## Hosted recovery verification

The planned free sandbox crash/restart at source `fedd609` completed D01 and D02 on their original
sessions after killing the first process immediately after its first journalled send. D01 scored
91.92% (session `99e5175b6c5630be`); D02 scored 46.09% (`2da225d3421b1101`). Both deals satisfied
must-haves and recorded zero timeouts. No replacement sessions were opened. Practice quota stayed
at 60 used / 140 left. Evidence is in the local ignored
`experiments/runs/integrated-free-recovery-fedd609/` directory. These are recovery observations,
not a paired comparison or proof of final-wave readiness.

Final local guards additionally cap contract option enumeration and charge document-fetch time
against recovered deadlines. They are covered by regression tests; the hosted run above precedes
those guards. The shared graph contract and module ownership are in
[the handoff](17-shared-memory-handoff.md).

## Limits

The model-backed interpreter/critic, automatic policy mutation and approved runtime lesson retrieval
are not enabled. Feedback proposes experiments; the lab's paired gates and explicit promotion still
decide policy adoption. New-release and final wave/host rehearsal remain release gates. The bounded
relationship search may reject an unsampled narrow feasible interval; it never fabricates a price.
General web news is not attached to fictional arena suppliers.

## Opt-in model interpretation candidate

`--model-assist` enables a short model read of each new supplier email. Set `LLM_PROVIDER`
(`anthropic` or `openai`), `LLM_MODEL`, and that provider's API key. The lab checkpoint stores
the provider and model name in its resolved configuration. A provider error, malformed JSON or
uncited extraction falls back to the existing deterministic parser. The async runner does the
bounded call outside its case decision lock; calls are cached per supplier message.

The model may extract objections, constraints, questions and proposed terms only when it cites
verbatim text from the current supplier email. Extracted terms carry `sheet_matched` or
`prose_only_unverified`; only the actual structured term sheet can be accepted. A cited index
objection can suppress that argument and select another verified claim. Template wording can
acknowledge selected concerns, but offers, prices, refs and closing decisions remain in code.

Optional live memory is read from `NEGOTIATOR_APPROVED_MEMORY` with
`NEGOTIATOR_DATA_SHA256` set to the lab data fingerprint. The snapshot must contain version 1
`lessons` with an exact supplier, case type, environment and data hash, valid-from/expiry,
approver, campaign, confidence and cited run/attempt evidence. Only explicitly approved lessons
are sent to the model; raw graph history and scores are never sent to the live agent. Barış's
graph service can replace this file adapter while retaining those filters. The model can cite
an approved lesson and summarize it as an observation; only its approved `avoid_claim_kind` may
change claim selection. No automatic lesson approval is implemented.

This candidate has local tests, including a full async simulator case. It has not passed a
hosted baseline/candidate campaign. Model quality, latency and token cost need measurement on
the actual provider before selection for a final run.

--- report ---
"""Run summaries for experiments (metrics in docs/04-experiments.md).

Sources, in order of authority: the run's trace.jsonl (our decisions and the result we saw),
hosted session dumps next to it (`hosted-<session>.json` from tools/replay_viewer.py, or the
`case-*.json` files of tools/sandbox_baseline.py: arena state with cost breakdown and threads),
and the sibling `<run>.log` for session ids. Every figure keeps a pointer to where it came from.

    uv run --locked python -m negotiator.report experiments/runs/practice_P01 [--json]
"""

import argparse
import json
import math
import re
import statistics
import sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

SESSION_RE = re.compile(r"\bsession ([0-9a-f]{16})\b")
GUARD_KEYS = ("guard", "guards", "blocked", "guard_outcome")


def find_traces(run_dir) -> list[Path]:
    p = Path(run_dir)
    if p.is_file():
        return [p]
    if (p / "trace.jsonl").is_file():
        return [p / "trace.jsonl"]
    return sorted(p.rglob("trace.jsonl"))


def load_trace(path) -> list[dict]:
    """Events of one trace.jsonl, each with `_src` = "<file>#L<n>". Bad lines are skipped."""
    out = []
    for n, line in enumerate(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), 1):
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        try:
            ev = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        ev["_src"] = f"{Path(path).name}#L{n}"
        out.append(ev)
    return out


def load_hosted(run_dir) -> dict[str, dict]:
    """case_id -> {"session", "state", "threads", "_src"} from hosted dumps in or above run_dir."""
    p = Path(run_dir)
    base = p.parent if p.is_file() else p
    out = {}
    for f in sorted(base.glob("*.json")):
        try:
            d = json.loads(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        except (json.JSONDecodeError, UnicodeDecodeError):
            continue
        if not isinstance(d, dict) or "state" not in d:
            continue
        state = d.get("state") or {}
        case = state.get("case_id") or d.get("case")
        if case:
            out[case] = {
                "session": d.get("session") or state.get("session_id"),
                "state": state,
                "threads": d.get("threads") or {},
                "_src": f.name,
            }
    return out


def session_ids(trace_path) -> list[str]:
    """Session ids from trace events, else from the sibling log (`runs/x/<ts>/trace.jsonl` -> `runs/x.log`)."""
    ids = []
    trace_path = Path(trace_path)
    for ev in load_trace(trace_path):
        for k in ("session", "session_id"):
            if isinstance(ev.get(k), str) and ev[k] not in ids:
                ids.append(ev[k])
    if ids:
        return ids
    run = trace_path.parent
    for log in (run.parent.with_suffix(".log"), run / "run.log", run.with_suffix(".log")):
        if log.is_file():
            for m in SESSION_RE.finditer(log.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")):
                if m.group(1) not in ids:
                    ids.append(m.group(1))
            if ids:
                break
    return ids


def _num(x):
    return x if isinstance(x, int | float) and not isinstance(x, bool) else None


def _decision(ev) -> dict:
    keep = ("kind", "supplier", "terms", "c", "c_alt", "reason", "sheet", "claims", "refs", "fallback", "latency_s")
    d = {k: ev[k] for k in keep if k in ev}
    for k in GUARD_KEYS:
        if k in ev:
            d["guard"] = ev[k]
    d["t"], d["src"] = ev.get("t"), ev["_src"]
    return d


def _case_summary(case_id, events, hosted) -> dict:
    decisions = [_decision(e) for e in events if e.get("event") == "decision"]
    results = [e for e in events if e.get("event") == "result"]
    guards = [
        {"src": e["_src"], **{k: v for k, v in e.items() if k not in ("t", "event", "case", "_src")}}
        for e in events
        if e.get("event") == "guard"
    ]
    guards += [
        {"src": d["src"], "kind": d["kind"], "supplier": d.get("supplier"), "outcome": d["guard"]}
        for d in decisions
        if "guard" in d
    ]
    claims = [
        {"src": d["src"], "supplier": d.get("supplier"), "claims": d.get("claims") or d.get("refs")}
        for d in decisions
        if d.get("claims") or d.get("refs")
    ]
    claims += [
        {"src": e["_src"], "supplier": e.get("supplier"), "claims": e.get("claims")}
        for e in events
        if e.get("event") == "evidence"
    ]
    offers = Counter(d.get("supplier") for d in decisions if d.get("kind") == "offer")
    s = {
        "case": case_id,
        "score": None,
        "deal": None,
        "supplier": None,
        "terms": None,
        "c_open": None,
        "c_deal": None,
        "c_best": None,
        "c_alt": next((d["c_alt"] for d in reversed(decisions) if _num(d.get("c_alt")) is not None), None),
        "gap": None,
        "components": None,
        "components_src": None,
        "must_haves_ok": None,
        "rounds": max(offers.values(), default=0),
        "offers_per_supplier": dict(offers),
        "decision_counts": dict(Counter(d.get("kind") for d in decisions)),
        "decisions": decisions,
        "guards": guards,
        "claims_used": claims,
        "fallbacks": sum(1 for d in decisions if d.get("fallback")),
        "error": None,
        "timeouts": None,
        "session": next(
            (
                e.get("session") or e.get("session_id")
                for e in events
                if isinstance(e.get("session") or e.get("session_id"), str)
            ),
            None,
        ),
        "replay_url": None,
        "result_src": None,
        "duration_s": None,
    }

    if results:
        r = results[-1]
        s["result_src"] = r["_src"]
        row = r.get("full") if isinstance(r.get("full"), dict) else r.get("result")
        if isinstance(row, dict):
            for k in ("score", "deal", "terms", "c_open", "c_deal", "c_best", "must_haves_ok"):
                if k in row:
                    s[k] = row[k]
            s["supplier"] = row.get("supplier_id")
            if isinstance(row.get("thread_timeouts"), dict) and row["thread_timeouts"]:
                s["timeouts"] = sum(row["thread_timeouts"].values())
            if row.get("score") is None or not isinstance(row.get("deal"), bool):
                s["error"] = "incomplete result"
            if isinstance(row.get("cost_breakdown"), dict):
                s["components"], s["components_src"] = row["cost_breakdown"], r["_src"]
        else:

        st = h["state"]
        res = st.get("result") or {}
        s["session"], s["replay_url"] = h.get("session") or s["session"], st.get("replay_url")
        if isinstance(st.get("rounds"), int):
            s["rounds"] = st["rounds"]
        for k in ("score", "deal", "terms", "c_open", "c_deal", "c_best", "c_alt", "must_haves_ok"):
            if s.get(k) is None and res.get(k) is not None:
                s[k] = res[k]
        if s["supplier"] is None:
            s["supplier"] = res.get("supplier_id")
        if s["components"] is None and isinstance(res.get("cost_breakdown"), dict):
            s["components"], s["components_src"] = res["cost_breakdown"], h["_src"]
        if h["threads"] and all("timeouts" in t for t in h["threads"].values()):
            s["timeouts"] = sum(len(t.get("timeouts") or []) for t in h["threads"].values())
    if not results and not h:
        s["error"] = "missing result"
    if s["error"] and "timeout" in s["error"].lower():
        s["timeouts"] = max(s["timeouts"] or 0, 1)
    if _num(s["c_deal"]) is not None and _num(s["c_best"]) is not None:
        s["gap"] = round(s["c_deal"] - s["c_best"], 2)
    return s


def summarise(run_dir) -> dict:
    """Per case: score, deal terms, C (open/deal/best/alt, components when the arena gave them),
    rounds, decisions, guard outcomes, claims used. Aggregate: mean/min score, worst case,
    deals, must-have breaks, failures, timeouts, fallbacks."""
    run_dir = Path(run_dir)
    traces = find_traces(run_dir)
    by_case: dict[str, tuple[str, list]] = {}  # key (case, or case#n for repeats) -> (case, events)
    runs, sessions = [], []
    for tr in traces:
        events = load_trace(tr)
        runs += [{k: v for k, v in e.items() if k != "event"} for e in events if e.get("event") == "run"]
        sessions += [x for x in session_ids(tr) if x not in sessions]
        for case in dict.fromkeys(e["case"] for e in events if e.get("case")):
            key, n = case, 2
            while key in by_case:
                key, n = f"{case}#{n}", n + 1
            by_case[key] = (case, [e for e in events if e.get("case") == case])
    hosted = {}
    for d in {run_dir} | {t.parent for t in traces}:
        hosted.update(load_hosted(d))
    cases = {key: _case_summary(case, events, hosted) for key, (case, events) in by_case.items()}
    for case_id in hosted:
        if case_id not in cases:
            cases[case_id] = _case_summary(case_id, [], hosted)
    single = [c for c in cases.values() if c["session"] is None]
    if len(sessions) == 1 and len(single) == 1:
        single[0]["session"] = sessions[0]
    for c in cases.values():

            c["replay_url"] = f"/replay/{c['session']}"
    scored = {k: c["score"] for k, c in cases.items() if _num(c["score"]) is not None}

"""v0.2 buyer: complete-cost packages, a price concession schedule and one checked close.

Every accept and walk-away goes through `evaluator.close_decision` (eligible sheets first, then
C with supplier estimates, against the alternative). Our non-price terms stay as offered unless a
supplier package evaluated by C is cheaper than its price for ours. No claims and no model yet.
"""

import logging
import math
import os
import time

from arena_kit.cost import closing_terms, complete_offer, must_haves_ok, total_cost
from arena_kit.docs import standard_terms
from arena_kit.play import latest, live_threads, moves_left

    best_close,
    close_decision,

log = logging.getLogger("negotiator")


def standing(case, events, supplier=None):
    """(term_sheet_id, terms) of the cheapest eligible sheet in the supplier's latest message, else
    of its cheapest priced sheet, else (None, {})."""
    cands = eligible_sheets(case, events, supplier, alternatives=True) or _priced(case, events, supplier)
    if cands:
        return cands[0][1], cands[0][2]
    sheets = latest(events).get("term_sheets") or [] if events else []
    return (sheets[0]["term_sheet_id"], sheets[0]["terms"]) if sheets else (None, {})


def _priced(case, events, supplier=None):
    """[(C, sheet_id, terms)] of every priced sheet in the latest message, must-haves ignored."""
    std = standard_terms(events)
    out = []
    for s in latest(events).get("term_sheets") or []:
        c = total_cost(case, s.get("terms") or {}, std, supplier)
        if s.get("term_sheet_id") and math.isfinite(c):
            out.append((c, s["term_sheet_id"], s["terms"]))
    return sorted(out, key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))


def load_estimates(case):
    """{supplier_id: estimate} from `dossiers.supplier_estimate` once it exists, else {}."""
    try:
        from .dossiers import supplier_estimate
    except ImportError:
        return {}
    out = {}
    for sid in case.get("suppliers", []):
        try:
            est = supplier_estimate(case, sid)
        except NotImplementedError:
            return {}
        except Exception:
            log.exception("supplier estimate for %s failed; using none", sid)
            continue
        if est:
            out[sid] = est
    return out


def _ceil2(x):
    return math.ceil(round(x * 100, 6)) / 100


class PackageAgent:
    version = "PackageAgent-v0.2"

    def __init__(
        self,
        anchor=0.12,
        rounds=5,
        close_gap=0.005,
        tracer=None,
        estimates=None,
        final_hold_s=40.0,
        meso=None,
        p_walk=0.25,
        claims=None,
        policy=None,
        model_assist=False,
        model_provider=None,
        model_name=None,
        memory=None,
        multi_supplier_anchor=None,
    ):
        self.anchor, self.rounds, self.close_gap, self.tracer = anchor, rounds, close_gap, tracer
        if multi_supplier_anchor is not None and (
            type(multi_supplier_anchor) not in (int, float)
            or not math.isfinite(multi_supplier_anchor)
            or not 0 <= multi_supplier_anchor < 1
        ):
            raise ValueError("multi_supplier_anchor must be a finite fraction below one")
        self.multi_supplier_anchor = multi_supplier_anchor
        if isinstance(policy, dict):
            from .policy import PolicyConfig

            policy = PolicyConfig.from_dict(policy)
        self.policy = policy
        self.package_advisor, self.package_notes = None, {}
        if policy and policy.package_advice_types:
            from .package_advisor import PackageAdvisor

            self.package_advisor = PackageAdvisor()
        self.memory = validate_memory(memory) if memory is not None else None
        self._memory_seen = set()
        self.conditional_exchange = False
        self.trades = None
        if policy:
            from .trades import TradePolicy

            self.trades = TradePolicy(policy, self._log)
        self.meso = os.environ.get("NEGOTIATOR_MESO") == "1" if meso is None else meso
        self.final_hold_s = final_hold_s
        self.p_walk = p_walk  # chance a supplier walks when its final offer is countered (D02: 2 of 9)
        self.claims = os.environ.get("NEGOTIATOR_CLAIMS") == "1" if claims is None else claims
        if policy is not None:
            self.claims = bool(policy.evidence_types or policy.recent_index_window_types)
        self.evidence = None
        self.model_context = {}
        self.model_seen = {}
        self.model_assist = None
        if model_assist:
            from .model_assist import ModelAssist

            self.model_assist = model_assist if isinstance(model_assist, ModelAssist) else ModelAssist(
                memory_path=os.environ.get("NEGOTIATOR_APPROVED_MEMORY"),
                data_sha256=os.environ.get("NEGOTIATOR_DATA_SHA256"),
                provider=model_provider, model=model_name,
            )
        if self.claims:
            from .evidence import EvidencePolicy

            self.evidence = EvidencePolicy(
                tracer=tracer, case_types=policy.evidence_types if policy else None,
                interpretation=self.model_context,
                recent_window_types=policy.recent_index_window_types if policy else (),
                rival_quote_types=policy.rival_quote_types if policy else (),
                index_window_types=policy.index_window_types if policy else ())
        self.prev = {}  # supplier -> non-price terms of our last offer
        self.final_counters = {}  # supplier -> counters sent to its final offers (at most one)
        self.beat_asked = {}  # rival supplier -> final-offer sheet id we asked it to beat
        self.reanchored = set()  # rfq suppliers re-anchored after undercutting our own ask
        self.final_seen = {}  # final-offer sheet id -> monotonic time first seen
        if estimates is None and os.environ.get("NEGOTIATOR_ESTIMATES") != "1":
            estimates = {}  # dossier estimates are opt-in until calibrated (docs: experiments/LOG.md)
        self._estimates, self._est_case, self._est_cache = estimates, None, {}
        self._target_cache = {}

    def prepare_email(self, case, threads, sid):
        """Read each supplier message once; the async runner calls this outside its lock."""
        if self.model_assist is None:
            return
        events = threads.get(sid, [])
        latest_supplier = next(((i, e) for i, e in reversed(list(enumerate(events)))
                                if e.get("from") != "buyer"), None)
        if latest_supplier is None:
            return
        from .ingestion import fingerprint

        token = (latest_supplier[0], fingerprint(latest_supplier[1]))
        if self.model_seen.get(sid) == token:
            return
        try:
            result = self.model_assist.read(case, events, sid)
        except Exception:
            from .replies import interpret

            result = {**interpret(events), "terms": [], "questions": [], "lessons": [], "source": "rules"}
        self.model_context[sid] = result
        self.model_seen[sid] = token
        self._log(case, "model_interpretation", sid, interpretation=result)

    def experiment_metrics(self):
        return {"model": self.model_assist.metrics() if self.model_assist is not None else
                {"calls": 0, "fallbacks": 0, "latency_s": [], "input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0},
                "memory_snapshot_id": self.memory["snapshot_id"] if self.memory else None}

    # -- estimates ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
    def estimates_for(self, case):
        """{supplier_id: estimate}: the injected estimates, else `dossiers.supplier_estimate`
        (with NEGOTIATOR_ESTIMATES=1)."""
        if self._estimates is not None:
            return self._estimates
        if self._est_case != case["case_id"]:
            self._est_case, self._est_cache = case["case_id"], load_estimates(case)
        return self._est_cache

    def _sup(self, case, threads, sid):
        return supplier_for(self.estimates_for(case), sid, standard_terms(threads[sid]))

    # -- helpers ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    @staticmethod
    def _ours(events):
        return [m["term_sheets"][0]["terms"] for m in events if m.get("from") == "buyer" and m.get("term_sheets")]

    def _log(self, case, kind, sid, **fields):
        if self.tracer:
            self.tracer.log("decision", case=case["case_id"], kind=kind, supplier=sid, **fields)

    def log_close(self, case, threads, decision, reason):
        best = best_close(case, threads, self.estimates_for(case))
        action = decision["message"]["action"]
        fields = {"c_alt": alternative_cost(case), "reason": reason}
        if action["type"] == "accept" and best:
            fields.update(c=best[0], sheet=action["term_sheet_id"])
        self._log(case, action["type"], decision["supplier_id"], **fields)

    def _close(self, case, threads, reason):
        decision = close_decision(case, threads, self.estimates_for(case), reason)
        self.log_close(case, threads, decision, reason)
        return decision

    def _offer(self, case, sid, terms, std, sup, c_alt, reason, variants=()):
        body = (
            f"Thank you for your offer. To go ahead we propose the attached terms: "
            f"unit price EUR {terms['unit_price']:.2f}"
            + "".join(f", {k.replace('_', ' ')} {v}" for k, v in terms.items() if k != "unit_price")
            + ". We look forward to your confirmation."
        )
        if self.trades and case["type"] in self.policy.package_types:
            if "contract_months" in terms:
                body += (
                    f" We offer a {terms['contract_months']}-month commitment"
                    + (
                        f" at annual volume {terms['volume_per_year']};"
                        if "volume_per_year" in terms
                        else " at unchanged annual volume;"
                    )
                    + " please reflect that commitment in your price, with payment priced as part of the package."
                )
            if "ppm_commitment" in terms:
                body += (
                    f" We can accept the proposed future quality commitment of {terms['ppm_commitment']} ppm"
                    " in exchange for the proposed price and chargeback terms."
                )
            body += (
                " This is a conditional exchange: we can commit to this package in return for the proposed unit price."
            )
        elif self.conditional_exchange and any(k != "unit_price" for k in terms):
            body += " The proposed non-price terms are conditional on the proposed unit price as one package."
        context = self.model_context.get(sid, {})
        signals = [x for x in context.get("signals", [])
                   if x.get("message_index") == self.model_seen.get(sid, (-1,))[0]]
        latest_signal = next(
            (x for x in reversed(signals) if x.get("kind") in
             {"payment_trade", "quality_objection", "delivery_constraint", "capacity_constraint"}),
            None,
        )
        if latest_signal:
            body += {
                "payment_trade": " We can consider payment terms as part of the full package.",
                "quality_objection": " We can discuss the quality requirements as part of this package.",
                "delivery_constraint": " Please clarify which delivery requirement is difficult to meet.",
                "capacity_constraint": " Please clarify the capacity you can commit to.",
            }[latest_signal["kind"]]
        if any(v.get("index_clause") != terms.get("index_clause") for v in variants):
            body += " Alternatively, please consider the attached packages; each is a separate proposal."
        assert not leaks(body), "body would leak internal information"
        self.prev[sid] = {k: v for k, v in terms.items() if k != "unit_price"}
        c = total_cost(case, terms, std, sup)
        sheets = [{"terms": t} for t in [terms, *variants][:3]]
        self._log(case, "offer", sid, terms=terms, c=c, c_alt=c_alt, reason=reason, variants=list(variants) or None)
        return {
            "supplier_id": sid,
            "message": {"subject": case["title"], "body": body, "term_sheets": sheets},
        }

    def _payment_variants(self, case, terms, theirs, std, sup):
        """Up to two sheets at our main sheet's C that differ only in payment days (the supplier's
        and the fastest option): the supplier picks the mix it values."""
        options = (case.get("term_options") or {}).get("payment_days") or []
        if "payment_days" not in terms or not options:
            return []
        c_main = total_cost(case, terms, std, sup)
        out = []
        for pay in (theirs.get("payment_days"), min(options)):
            if pay is None or pay == terms["payment_days"] or pay in [v["payment_days"] for v in out]:
                continue
            v = {**terms, "payment_days": pay}
            v["unit_price"] = math.floor(price_for_cost(case, v, c_main, std, sup) * 100) / 100
            if must_haves_ok(case, v, std):
                out.append(complete_offer(case, v))
        return out

    def _clause_on(self, case):
        return bool(self.policy and case["type"] in self.policy.clause_variant_types)

    @staticmethod
    def _clause_probed(events):
        """True once one of our messages carried sheets that differ in index_clause."""
        for m in events:
            if m.get("from") == "buyer" and len(m.get("term_sheets") or []) > 1:
                if len({repr(s["terms"].get("index_clause")) for s in m["term_sheets"]}) > 1:
                    return True
        return False

    def _clause_track(self, case, sid, events, prev, ref_terms):
        """Locked previous terms, except for the index clause when clause variants are enabled:
        a mandatory clause (we offered none; every latest supplier sheet carries one) adopts the
        supplier's clause, and after our deadband probe the cheapest supplier sheet's (by C)
        clause is adopted. Never insists on no clause."""
        if not self._clause_on(case) or "index_clause" not in prev:
            return prev
        sheets = latest(events).get("term_sheets") or []
        clause = ref_terms.get("index_clause")
        if clause is None or clause not in (case.get("term_options") or {}).get("index_clause", []):
            return prev
        mandatory = prev["index_clause"] is None and sheets and all(s["terms"].get("index_clause") for s in sheets)
        if (mandatory or self._clause_probed(events)) and clause != prev["index_clause"]:
            self._log(case, "clause_track", sid, prev=prev["index_clause"], new=clause, mandatory=bool(mandatory))
            return {**prev, "index_clause": clause}
        return prev

    def _clause_variants(self, case, events, terms, std, sup):
        """Once, after the supplier made the clause mandatory: up to two sheets at our main sheet's
        C that differ only in deadband (legal options of the same series), so the supplier reveals
        which deadband it prices cheaper."""
        clause = terms.get("index_clause")

            if o and o.get("series") == clause.get("series") and o != clause

"""Versioned, explicit experiment settings. Omitted config preserves legacy behavior."""

import hashlib
import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Literal

TYPES = {"price_increase", "renewal", "rfq", "bundling", "raw_material", "capacity", "quality"}


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PolicyConfig:
    version: int = 1
    package_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    evidence_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    final_offer_risk: str = "legacy"
    preference: str = "default"
    chargeback_steps: int = 1
    preferences: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    cost_neutral_lead_time: bool = False
    package_advice_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cost_target_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cost_target_index_clause: bool = False
    # Restrict the relationship-cost target to the shortest legal payment option. The target
    # price is still derived from the public supplier-cost model and the complete buyer cost.
    cost_target_fast_payment: bool = False
    clause_variant_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    rfq_nonleading_hold: bool = False
    rfq_final_guard: bool = False
    # Case types whose opening and later packages keep the supplier's standard (quote PDF)
    # payment days when that is a listed option; price is still scheduled by buyer C.
    standard_payment_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    rfq_supplier_lead_time: bool = False
    rfq_rival_offer: bool = False
    rfq_supplier_payment: bool = False
    rfq_rival_offer_history: bool = False
    rfq_undercut_reanchor: bool = False
    rfq_data_claims: bool = False
    rfq_data_claims_stack: bool = False
    # Case types whose evidence uses only public index windows ending at the latest month.
    recent_index_window_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    rival_quote_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    index_window_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cost_target_posterior: float = 0.0  # s_max of the in-session supplier-cost posterior; 0 = off
    # Case types whose opening takes the longest contract term among options of equal buyer C
    # (e.g. a commitment beyond the cost horizon) and keeps it against equal-cost shortening.
    longer_tenor_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    # Per case type opening anchor (fraction below the supplier's price); others use the agent's.
    anchor_by_type: dict[str, float] = field(default_factory=dict)
    # Case types whose offers state, from public facts, the volume a kit moves to the supplier
    # (kit memo quantities x need, current sourcing quota, forecast IDs, capacity note).
    bundle_volume_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    # Subset of bundle_volume_types whose later offers answer the supplier's volume question with the
    # case's fixed volume over the offered term and, if it has a pricing committee, the approval path.
    bundle_commitment_types: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    # Per case type number of buyer rounds over which the price schedule reaches the
    # supplier's price (faster convergence before a supplier's final offer); others use the agent's.
    rounds_by_type: dict[str, int] = field(default_factory=dict)

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, path):
        return cls.from_dict(json.loads(Path(path).read_text()))

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data):
        d = dict(data) if isinstance(data, dict) else data
        if not isinstance(d, dict) or set(d) - set(cls.__dataclass_fields__):
            raise ValueError("unknown policy fields")
        if type(d.get("version")) is not int or d["version"] != 1:
            raise ValueError("policy version must be 1")
        for k in (
            "package_types",
            "evidence_types",
            "package_advice_types",
            "cost_target_types",
            "clause_variant_types",
            "standard_payment_types",
            "recent_index_window_types",
            "rival_quote_types",
            "index_window_types",
            "longer_tenor_types",
            "bundle_volume_types",
            "bundle_commitment_types",
        ):
            v = d.get(k, [])
            if not isinstance(v, list) or any(not isinstance(x, str) or x not in TYPES for x in v):
                raise ValueError(f"invalid {k}")
            d[k] = tuple(sorted(set(v)))
        for k in ("cost_neutral_lead_time", "cost_target_index_clause", "cost_target_fast_payment",
                  "rfq_nonleading_hold", "rfq_final_guard",
                  "rfq_supplier_lead_time", "rfq_rival_offer", "rfq_supplier_payment", "rfq_rival_offer_history",
                  "rfq_undercut_reanchor", "rfq_data_claims", "rfq_data_claims_stack"):
            if type(d.get(k, False)) is not bool:
                raise ValueError(f"{k} must be boolean")
        post = d.get("cost_target_posterior", 0.0)
        if isinstance(post, bool) or not isinstance(post, (int, float)) or not 0 <= post <= 1:
            raise ValueError("cost_target_posterior must be a number in [0, 1]")
        d["cost_target_posterior"] = float(post)
        if d.get("final_offer_risk", "legacy") not in ("legacy", "opening_proxy"):
            raise ValueError("invalid final_offer_risk")
        if d.get("preference", "default") not in ("default", "standard_payment", "longer_tenor", "lower_chargeback"):
            raise ValueError("invalid preference")
        steps = d.get("chargeback_steps", 1)
        if type(steps) is not int or not 1 <= steps <= 3:
            raise ValueError("chargeback_steps must be 1, 2 or 3")
        preferences = d.get("preferences", {})
        allowed = {"default", "standard_payment", "longer_tenor", "lower_chargeback"}
        if not isinstance(preferences, dict) or any(
            k not in TYPES or not isinstance(v, str) or v not in allowed for k, v in preferences.items()
        ):
            raise ValueError("invalid case-type preferences")
        anchors = d.get("anchor_by_type", {})
        if not isinstance(anchors, dict) or any(
            k not in TYPES or type(v) not in (int, float) or not 0 <= v <= 0.4 for k, v in anchors.items()
        ):
            raise ValueError("invalid anchor_by_type")
        d["anchor_by_type"] = {k: float(v) for k, v in anchors.items()}
        rounds = d.get("rounds_by_type", {})
        if not isinstance(rounds, dict) or any(
            k not in TYPES or type(v) is not int or not 1 <= v <= 12 for k, v in rounds.items()
        ):
            raise ValueError("invalid rounds_by_type")
        d["rounds_by_type"] = dict(rounds)
        return cls(**d)

    def record(self):
        d = asdict(self)
        return {"config": d, "sha256": hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(d, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()}

# Integrated harve/y runtime and lab

Implementation on `codex/harvey-integrated-runtime`, based on main `dc3a109` and lab `08274aa`.
The original development checkout and its local credentials remain separate.

## Implemented

- Unconfirmed closes raise an incomplete-session error without writing a finished journal result.
  Resume keeps the existing session. Exhausted uncertain sends retain their persisted move ID.
  Cached replies keep server-derived remaining time; worker failures reach the caller.
- Main's package policies and shared closing evaluator are retained. `economics.evaluate` rejects
  invalid prices/options/fixed-term changes/must-haves and returns full components plus demand coverage.
  Price-budget search handles non-monotonic relationship costs with bounded sampling and validates
  rounded prices. Sampling is conservative; it does not claim a global optimum.
- Versioned public ingestion records file hashes, case context and explicit source conflicts.
  Conflicting release IDs are excluded from claims. Missing optional tables produce diagnostics;
  explicit missing data paths do not silently load a different package. Contact notes and
  previously unknown suppliers are retained. Prep output includes the data manifest.
- Bounded extractive reply interpretation identifies supplier statements about hedging, payment,
  quality, clauses and authority. Verified alternative arguments replace vetoed index arguments.
  Final offers receive no new evidence decoration. This implementation uses deterministic rules,
  not an LLM or personality inference; it makes zero provider calls.
- The lab accepts embedded validated policy configurations in immutable checkpoints, so its worker
  can execute the same package policy as the normal CLI. Workers retain decision traces.
- `FeedbackAgent` audits original outcomes and conversations and emits referenced keep/change/test
  findings. Recovered scores remain separate, unknown timeouts stay unknown, and uncovered demand
  triggers a contract comparison recommendation. Matching versioned public data enables qualified
  offer checks; unknown historical versions are skipped rather than checked against today's data.
  Cross-run observations are retained as observations, never auto-approved runtime policy.
- Feedback is available from the authenticated `/api/feedback/<run_id>` read endpoint and in each
  dashboard experiment's Decision feedback disclosure. CLI audits are stored separately from
  immutable attempt records and can be regenerated.

## Use the integrated candidate

```sh
uv run --locked negotiator play case:D01 --runner async --policy-config configs/candidate.json
uv run --locked negotiator lab feedback --data "$ARENA_DATA"
```

The first command starts a free hosted sandbox session when configured for the arena. The second
only audits the local lab database. Do not run practice as an incidental verification command.

For a lab checkpoint, pass `configs/harvey-lab-checkpoint.json` as the config and select `--runner async`.
Use the explicit `configs/lab-async-sandbox-suite.json` suite and a matching base data manifest.
That suite has three repeats per case per arm: twelve free sandbox sessions, not two. Publication,
baseline seeding, family budget and campaign execution remain explicit actions using the lab CLI.
The committed base hash matches the audited kit data; a new release requires a new manifest/suite.

Local end-to-end rehearsal:

```sh
uv run --locked python tools/rehearse_loop.py --runner async \
  --policy configs/candidate.json --data "$ARENA_DATA"
```

This creates an isolated temporary lab, local Git remote and kit simulator, then runs twelve local
sessions through restored checkpoints. It does not change the shared lab recommendation or use
hosted quota. Its deliberately weak control tests integration, not production competitiveness.

## Imported evidence

The integration checkout's ignored `experiments/dashboard.sqlite3` contains 100 run records / 113
attempts: the two saved practice sweeps (15 attempts), plus 53 sandbox and 45 additional practice
sessions read from owned history. Fifteen existing practice sessions were deduplicated. No import
failures. Original source/config is unknown for server-only history, and the importer is not the
original author. P10's operator-assisted recovery preserves its original failed execution.

This is a local database. It has not replaced Barış's running shared database or deployed the UI.
Use the existing lab sync workflow with the team's configured destination when publishing records.
Keep credentials and the local derived feedback JSON out of Git.

## Hosted recovery verification

The planned free sandbox crash/restart at source `fedd609` completed D01 and D02 on their original
sessions after killing the first process immediately after its first journalled send. D01 scored
91.92% (session `99e5175b6c5630be`); D02 scored 46.09% (`2da225d3421b1101`). Both deals satisfied
must-haves and recorded zero timeouts. No replacement sessions were opened. Practice quota stayed
at 60 used / 140 left. Evidence is in the local ignored
`experiments/runs/integrated-free-recovery-fedd609/` directory. These are recovery observations,
not a paired comparison or proof of final-wave readiness.

Final local guards additionally cap contract option enumeration and charge document-fetch time
against recovered deadlines. They are covered by regression tests; the hosted run above precedes
those guards. The shared graph contract and module ownership are in
[the handoff](17-shared-memory-handoff.md).

## Limits

The model-backed interpreter/critic, automatic policy mutation and approved runtime lesson retrieval
are not enabled. Feedback proposes experiments; the lab's paired gates and explicit promotion still
decide policy adoption. New-release and final wave/host rehearsal remain release gates. The bounded
relationship search may reject an unsampled narrow feasible interval; it never fabricates a price.
General web news is not attached to fictional arena suppliers.

## Opt-in model interpretation candidate

`--model-assist` enables a short model read of each new supplier email. Set `LLM_PROVIDER`
(`anthropic` or `openai`), `LLM_MODEL`, and that provider's API key. The lab checkpoint stores
the provider and model name in its resolved configuration. A provider error, malformed JSON or
uncited extraction falls back to the existing deterministic parser. The async runner does the
bounded call outside its case decision lock; calls are cached per supplier message.

The model may extract objections, constraints, questions and proposed terms only when it cites
verbatim text from the current supplier email. Extracted terms carry `sheet_matched` or
`prose_only_unverified`; only the actual structured term sheet can be accepted. A cited index
objection can suppress that argument and select another verified claim. Template wording can
acknowledge selected concerns, but offers, prices, refs and closing decisions remain in code.

Optional live memory is read from `NEGOTIATOR_APPROVED_MEMORY` with
`NEGOTIATOR_DATA_SHA256` set to the lab data fingerprint. The snapshot must contain version 1
`lessons` with an exact supplier, case type, environment and data hash, valid-from/expiry,
approver, campaign, confidence and cited run/attempt evidence. Only explicitly approved lessons
are sent to the model; raw graph history and scores are never sent to the live agent. Barış's
graph service can replace this file adapter while retaining those filters. The model can cite
an approved lesson and summarize it as an observation; only its approved `avoid_claim_kind` may
change claim selection. No automatic lesson approval is implemented.

This candidate has local tests, including a full async simulator case. It has not passed a
hosted baseline/candidate campaign. Model quality, latency and token cost need measurement on
the actual provider before selection for a final run.

			75 content list
				76 container

Then  uv run arena-sim serve --final-rehearsal --data data/package  and in a second terminal  ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Rehearsal" sim  and  ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 ARENA_API_KEY=<key> uv run arena run --set final --waves 2 --agent llm --parallel 10 . It plays two short waves with the real rules: the  403  wait, the wave start, one session per case,  seconds_left , the cap. Own client? Point it at the same URL.
				79 container
					80 AXListMarker • 
					81 text 09:00 pre-flight on arena.tacto.ai:  one practice case on your final machine, key and network - then start your final runner for a minute. It must  wait : until wave 1 starts, the final case list answers  403 .
				82 container
					83 AXListMarker • 
					84 text Own client? 403  before wave 1 means "keep waiting". One session per case: a second  POST /v1/sessions  is a  409  - pick up the running one. Read  seconds_left . HTTP timeout ≥ 180 s, retry  429  after  Retry-After . New suppliers: don't assume the practice ones. Easiest: plug your agent into the kit's  play_waves() .
				85 container
					86 AXListMarker • 
					87 text By 11:55:  stop your practice loops. Practice sessions count against your 10 open sessions and can block wave 1.
				88 container
					89 AXListMarker • 
					90 text Before 12:00:  start  uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10  (or your own runner) and leave it running until the fifth wave has closed. Code + slides freeze on ehl.gg at 12:00.
				91 container
					92 AXListMarker • 
					93 text The cap - your call:  each wave has 8 minutes; whatever is still open then ends without a deal. The kit plays safe: 90 seconds before the cap it stops countering and takes the best standing offer that beats your alternative, else walks. That margin is one constant,  CLOSE_BEFORE_CAP_S = 90  in  arena_kit/play.py  - change it if you like. Mind that a supplier's reply can take up to about a minute, longer under the final's load, and a reply that arrives after the cap is lost.
				94 container
					95 AXListMarker • 
					96 text During the final: hands off.  Restarting a crashed runner is fine - it picks up its sessions. Picking cases or writing messages by hand is not, and your agent must not read the leaderboard, the screen or the event feed.

					107 text Your deal becomes one number in €.  The term sheet you accept is priced as its  total cost C : what it costs to cover your need over the case's horizon, at the case's published rates.

						136 text Supplier's health
					137 cell
						138 text strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point you leave the supplier below a sustainable margin
			139 content list

					141 AXListMarker 2. 
					142 text The score compares your deal with the opening and the best possible deal.
					143 container score equals C open minus C deal, divided by C open minus C best, clipped to 0 to 1
					144 definition list

--- measured demo ---
# Measured demo for the team

These are hosted practice results, not a forecast of the final or jury prize.

## Lead with the decision

The agent negotiates the package, not just unit price. It calculates buyer cost in code,
uses verified supplier-specific facts, and keeps fixed terms private and unchanged.

## P04: buy the commitment the supplier values

The supplier dossier says discounts require a multi-year agreement. The baseline kept a
12-month agreement and scored 5.64. The candidate offered 24 months at the same annual
20,000 units, negotiated EUR 4.94 with 90-day payment, and scored 86.04. A fresh paired
confirmation reproduced both numbers. Complete cost fell from EUR 198,715.67 to 196,852.67.

Show [the measured replay](../experiments/replays/p04-package-evidence.html). The delivery
claim was verified, but package-only achieved the same score; do not attribute the gain to
that claim. The evidence supports the package trade as the useful change in this experiment.

## P11: price the penalty instead of demanding it for free

The supplier repeatedly charged for a high chargeback. The baseline obtained EUR 48.00
with EUR 500 chargeback and scored 31.44. The selected refinement started with a permitted
lower chargeback and later traded it to zero for a lower price. It closed at EUR 45.50,
300 ppm, zero chargeback, with payment still fixed at 60 days: score 70.99, repeated once.

The complete-cost evaluator explicitly charges EUR 2,146.50 for residual defects. It still
prefers the cheaper package: C = EUR 750,082.50 versus the baseline EUR 787,686. The actual
historical 2,376 ppm and electricity-index claims were verified. Historical defects and the
future 300 ppm commitment are different facts. The agent ignored supplier requests to
negotiate payment, because that field is fixed in this case.

Show [the measured replay](../experiments/replays/p11-chargeback-evidence.html), the supplier's
chargeback objection, our conditional package change, and the complete cost breakdown.

## What we can claim

These gains repeated, with valid deals, zero actual thread timeouts and no contradicted claims.
Exact repeats may be cached, so they demonstrate reproducibility rather than significance.
One frozen ten-case comparison is still required before claiming the combined policy improves
its mean without material regressions. Final wave/recovery and Sunday release readiness are
separate gates. The overall jury prize is not determined by these practice scores alone.

## 2026-10-10 — P02 in-session supplier-cost posterior (branch `codex/score-push-fullcost-rel`)

Hypothesis (coordinator): the instant accept of 366.23 / 90 d / CU db5 is runtime evidence that the
supplier's cost sits below the public prior midpoint 374.95, so the cost target should adapt.

Offline (no session; `/tmp/fc2/p02_post.py`, public dossier prior fc ~ U[356.20, 393.70]):
- Likelihood: the supplier accepts an offer worth v to it (`supplier_value`) iff v >= fc·(1−s),
  s ~ U[0, s_max] (how far below full cost it will sell). 366.23/90d is worth 361.35 to it.
- Posterior after an accept at 366.23, and the E[C]-optimal price on the same package:
  s_max .10 → E[fc] 370.3, opt 362.10; .125 → 371.6, 363.05; **.15 → 372.3, 363.65**; .20 → 373.1,

  at 349.37 in 5eccc847 (worth 344.71 to it), so acceptance alone does not bound fc from below.
  It only says s is large (≥ 6 % at fc 366.7).
- Score range at fc points (local model; hosted was ~.026 below local at 366.23). Price 363.37 vs 366.23:
  fc 356 +1.25/+0.89, fc 362 +1.10/+0.86, fc 366.7 **+0.74/+0.63**, fc 375 −0.47/−0.34,

  score at fc ≈ 375 and ~.05 at fc ≈ 385. A refusal-driven posterior would also over-concede: one
  counter at 363.37 lifts E[fc] to 382 and the optimum to 375. So refusals may only bring us back to
  the prior optimum, never above it.

  No P10 session.

What differs from previous P02 attempts (5eccc847 cost-driver, p02-cost-target 366.23 → .5993):

optimum, never above it. It accepts a supplier sheet on our package at or below that price.

# How To Present A Successful Hackathon Demo

Brandon Kessler

8:00 PM PDT · September 1, 2014

Editor’s note: Brandon Kessler is the founder and CEO of ChallengePost, a platform to showcase software, online competitions, and hackathons.

It’s sad to stay up for three days building something awesome only to bomb the demo presentation. It’s no surprise it happens: you’re exhausted and racing to finish your project, with little time to plan your words, and only a few minutes to say them. So here’s some advice on how to give a great hackathon presentation.

1. Quickly set the scene

Why did you build this? In a few sentences, explain the problem you’re solving, or the status quo you’re greatly improving. The more the audience grasps the problem, the better. But remember, keep it short and to the point.

Some examples: “We all know doing math homework is a total drag, so… I created a robot to do it.” Or, “Urban planning is one of the most complex professions in the world. The tools on the market are expensive, outdated, and use two dimensions when the world has moved to 3D. I wanted to change that.”

2. Demo your working project

Now that you’ve set the scene, it’s time for the most important part: showing your project in action. Decide what’s important to show within the time you’re allotted. Briefly mention key technologies you used, or impressive technical challenges you overcame. Skip mundane flows such as creating user credentials, and have any needed text copied to your clipboard. Whatever you do, it’s crucial to show resolution to the problem you initially identified so your audience can see a) what your project does, and b) that you’ve completed the key components of it.

3. Quickly wrap it up and sell the dream

Now that you’ve shown your project actually helps solve the problem you identified, spend a sentence or two highlighting its potential and any ambitions you have, so your audience understands its long-term impact.

4. Crush your online presentation

Most hackathons require you to submit your projects online first so you get maximum exposure, and because judges use the platform to determine finalists. Start early as it will pay dividends and help you crystallize your thoughts. Like your verbal demo, a great online presentation will describe the problem you’re solving, show what the hack specifically does, and highlight its potential impact.

You should mention the technologies you used, anything interesting you learned, and give credit to your teammates. The best presentations we see on our platform include screenshots and a video demo. And remember, just because the hackathon ends, you don’t have to stop hacking. Keep updating your project so your fans stay in the loop.

Good luck!

# A Guide to Demo Day Presentations

July 25, 2016·by Geoff Ralston

In 2005 Y Combinator held its first Demo Day. Eight companies showed off their products and sold their vision to an audience of about 15 investors. Today, accelerators and incubators around the world hold their own demo days, and in 2016 over 200 YC companies will describe their startups to an audience of hundreds. Creating an effective demo day presentation has become an important part of participating in YC, not just due to the importance of Demo Day, but because the very process of fashioning the presentation is valuable. Surprisingly, it can be the first time founders achieve clarity together and come to a shared understanding of their story.^{1}

Since that first YC batch we’ve helped over 1000 companies with their presentations. This guide summarizes what we’ve learned and describes how to create an effective demo day presentation. It is the perfect companion to A Guide to Seed Fundraising, where we discuss the mechanics of raising seed capital.^{2}

While reading this guide keep in mind that a short presentation to investors will seldom convince any of them to invest on the spot. This is especially true when the presentation is one of many. In that case, investors are simply trying to manage the flow of information and, more than anything else, figure out who they can ignore and who they’d like to meet. Therefore, your goal should be to intrigue your listeners enough that they will want to meet you and learn more. Keep that goal in mind and follow the prescriptions below, and you are much more likely to have a great demo day.

For readers without the time or inclination to read even this short manual, I’ll give up the secret to a great presentation now: practice. Make sure you know your story so well that it comes out as smoothly as a Steve Jobs pitch. It turns out that the very process of working thoroughly and intensively on your story will force you to improve it and make it more persuasive.

There is a more extensive reading list at the end of this post, but must-reads include:
• How to Present to Investors by Paul Graham^{3}
• How to Design a Better Pitch Deck by Kevin Hale^{4}
• Advice on Pitching by Aaron Harris^{5}

Your Presentation
Like all presentations, your demo day presentation is a story. Each founder will have occasion to act as a salesperson for their company and to tell that story–this is a chance for everyone to get on the same page. Your presentation should be the culmination of an effort to synthesize and understand as deeply as possible your core message, your opportunity, and, especially, the product you are building. The very best demo day presentations have four core qualities:

• Clarity – the presentation is clearly and simply presented.
• Excitement – the opportunity is compelling; it demands listeners pay attention.
• Informative – it teaches listeners something they did not know.
• Memorable – your story stays with the audience; later they can recall who you are and what you do.

The best technique to achieve these qualities is a process of repetition, critique, and editing (including, importantly, selective removal). But in order to build your presentation you need to start with a framework. We call this the story’s vertebrae.

Vertebrae
Most listeners will remember – at most – 3 or 4 key points from a presentation they have just heard, especially if it is one presentation out of many. The vertebrae of a presentation are those points. They will be the most compelling and memorable ways to describe the company and its opportunity. These are not necessarily the points that explain what the company does, but rather those that will be most likely to pique the attention of your audience and convince them that they want to learn more. The presentation is then constructed to convey these points as effectively as possible.

A great way to derive these four points is via the Socratic method. Ask yourselves:
• What are we building and for whom?
• Why hasn’t this been done before?
• Why is it hard to do what we are doing?
• Why is this an opportunity not to be missed?

It is helpful to begin your story as narrowly as you can and then expand upon that simple story only as far as you need to and no further. The best presentation will be complete yet concise: a story told with great clarity.

The Audience
The goal of any presenter is to capture an audience’s attention and bring them along through their story. The very best presenters are captivating, informative, provocative, and sometimes funny. The worst are painfully awkward, convoluted, boring, or all of these.

The first step to success is to know to whom you are speaking. Or, rather, to know what it is that speaks to the people in front of you. Investors care only to find the next hot startup, and your goal is to convince them that it might just be you. Unfortunately, you usually have a distressingly short time in which to do this. This is true regardless of the length allotted to your presentation, since most investors will tune out almost instantly.

It turns out that investors have a much easier time deciding which startups they do not like. Since this is the easier path they do it first, and thus their initial goal is to decide which startups they do not have to talk to. This makes their main goal much simpler – to decide which startups they must meet.

A presentation that is built to make a company impossible to ignore, that actually instills fear in investors that missing this opportunity might mean missing the next Airbnb, is most likely to get you that next meeting and a chance to close a deal. All investors, angels, and venture capitalists alike have a deep fear of missing out on the next big thing when it is right in front of them.

Presentation Organization
Demo day presentations tend to follow a consistent structure, but there is also plenty of room for variation, especially for experienced presenters. Here is an outline of the usual components, though the order of how you present them is up to you; in most cases the introduction will come first and the conclusion at the end, though sometimes we advise companies to show impressive traction on the very first slide, and that is all it will take to grab the audience’s attention and hold it. I’ve heard my colleague Justin Kan yell, “Don’t bury the lead,” when a founder finishes with the fact that they have $5mm in revenue and are profitable, rather than starting with that fact.

The Introduction
This is not much different from the so-called elevator pitch. Briefly say what you are doing and why. It is especially helpful to start off by saying as clearly as you can what you are in terms that the audience is likely to understand. For example, “We deliver groceries to customers in their homes,” is clearer than “we are a next generation, AI-based resolver of grocery needs.” This is sometimes called a mission statement, but regardless, strive for conciseness and clarity. A common error is to avoid describing what you do until far into the presentation. That is always a mistake.

The Problem You Are Solving
In almost every case, a simple description of the problem your product solves should be a part of your presentation. However, beware of the caveat above, and do not spend too much time describing your problem leading up to your fantastic solution, and leaving the listener wondering what, exactly, you do until half your pitch is done.

The Product and the Customer
Explain in more detail what you are building and for whom. This used to be where you would show a demo, but ironically, demos seldom work in modern demo day presentations. Explaining rapidly and clearly what your product does can be the most challenging, and rewarding part of getting ready for a demo day.

Preparation
After coaching founders on hundreds of demo day presentations, there is really only one preparation technique that matters, and luckily it is dead simple: practice. And after you’ve practiced, practice some more. Not only will your delivery improve, but, and this is no less important, you and your co-founders will eventually discover what works and does not work on your own, just from listening and relistening to your own ideas as to why your company will be a massive success.

Practicing with co-founders and/or others is, in fact, vital to your success. Most of you will have no idea what you sound like nor the mistakes you will make when you first practice your presentation. You may speak too loudly, too softly or too quickly. Practice in front of people who will give you honest, unvarnished feedback. If you don’t have people to practice with, record yourself and watch the recordings.

Who Should Present
One person should give the presentation. We strongly recommend against switching back and forth between presenters. It is also terribly easy to overcomplicate this choice. The presenter does not have to be the CEO or the person with the most equity. Simply choose the presenter who presents the best. A demo day presentation is not about glory, it is about generating the most interest possible. Choose the team member who speaks most clearly, with the most confidence, and makes the most persuasive case for your company.

Technique
Every speaker has their own technique and it is important to be authentic. Yes, you are acting, but few of us are good enough to act convincingly as another person. Those who are that skilled probably don’t need to read this part of the guide. The rest of us need to find our own voice, our own passion, and our own inner storyteller. However, there are some common qualities shared by all great speakers from which you can learn:

• Be confident and enthusiastic. Show your passion.
• Project. This is especially important if you are speaking to a large crowd, but will always make you more impressive, signal greater passion, and make you more easily understood.
• Smile, but not too much. It will not only make you seem more relaxed and confident, it will make you more relaxed and confident.
• Speak slowly. We advise founders to speak unnaturally slowly, especially if they talk fast habitually. By the way, this is especially important in a demo day presentation because your listeners are absorbing such a huge amount of information, they need extra time to process what you are saying.
• Pause from time to time. A pause is powerful – it forces the audience to pay attention, forces you to slow down, and gives you time to gather your thoughts.
• Speak clearly. Especially if you are not presenting in your native tongue. • Speak with cadence. With practice, even a memorized script can become more natural and interesting. A monotone, robotic delivery will put your audience to sleep.
• Stand or move naturally. Don’t be stiff. However, don’t move too much. Do not pace. Do not dance! See below for more tips on movement.

Movement
An important part of appearing confident, powerful, and formidable up on stage is how you move during your talk. It is almost never a good idea to be completely static. Your should be as natural as possible and not stand like a statue. An unmoving founder will often leave investors equally unmoved. Equally important is not to move too much so that you distract your audience.

Most of the time you should stand with your feet planted firmly and your weight equally distributed. Try not to shift your weight as that will cause you to sway distractingly. Similarly, although it is perfectly fine to move, do not pace. Take a few steps, stop, talk for a while, then move again if you like.

Always face your audience. Avoid turning to look at your slides. Your presence is diminished each time you lose eye contact with your audience. If you want to point at something, do so while facing towards the front. If you are not sure you are on the right slide and there is no monitor in front of you, you can check, but trust your clicker and don’t do this on every slide.

Generally, repetitive movement is a distraction to the audience whether it is pacing or swinging your arm at each point you make or each time you make a slide transition.

It is very difficult to give your presentation and pay attention to all these things simultaneously. The best way to improve is to have others give you feedback and work to eliminate bad habits on each iteration. It is also very useful to record yourself and watch what you do.

Common Errors
As you practice and refine your presentation, refer back to this list to make sure you aren’t making any classic presenter mistakes. Some of the most common errors we see include:

• Muddying, or leaving out entirely, a description of the problem you are solving and how you are solving it – in other words not communicating what you are doing. This description should be covered very early in your presentation.
• Using jargon, unnecessarily complex phrasing or descriptions, or marketing boilerplate. E.g.. “Our SaaS product provides customers the complex analytical solutions for their enterprise big data needs.”
• Exaggerating the truth. Exaggerations, or worse, outright untruths, are fatal errors.
• Completing your presentations without leaving investors with a clear idea as to why they should care.
• Screen vs. presenter disease – where the audience cannot figure out whether to pay attention to your slides or you, but they are forced to choose.
• Looking at your slides when talking. Face your audience and project to them. Here, as always, practice helps.
• Saying too many words, especially if they are complex or buzzwordy. Listeners get “buffer overflow” and forget everything. Then, they read email. Talking too fast. Talking in front of a lot of people is different than talking one on one.
• Including a slide that does not help investors invest in you. For example, “That’s nuts!” and for that exclamation including a slide with a picture of nuts.
• Including complex graphs.
• Including a video. They are almost never a good idea – investors are there to judge you and therefore want to see you perform live.
• Dancing: it is hard to present like a superstar, but we can learn from superstar presenters. Look how they move. They do not shift from foot to foot or jump jerkily from position to position or, especially, throw their hands and arms around much. They move in deliberate, confident strides and often stop and stare directly into the audience to make a point.
• Plowing through without pause. It is important to pace your talk. Not only do you need to breathe, but so does your audience. In fact, if you do not pause, you miss an opportunity to emphasize your most important points.
• Your approach to your presentation tells listeners a ton about you. If you seem bored or angry or anything but confident and passionate about your idea, your chance of winning them over is next to zero.

content.text:
Initial read: the strongest story is not “we used an LLM to negotiate.” It is “we turn every offer into a comparable total-cost decision, show the evidence, and keep the model outside the authority boundary.” The live lab already supports that story through experiment comparison, score history, and memory, but it currently has no seeded runs on this local preview, so it cannot be the only proof surface.

For three minutes, I recommend a six-slide arc: stakes → full-cost insight → decision architecture → one recorded replay → measured evidence → live lab/close. The screen demo should be a short, rehearsed reveal, with a slide-based replay ready as an instant fallback. That keeps the product central without risking a blank state or network timing.
